The New Sociology of Science as the Foundation of the Epistemic Process: A Coherence–Persistence Rereading of Auguste Comte
Authors/Creators
Kriger, Boris
Description
The canonical reading of Auguste Comte places sociology at the apex of a hierarchical classification of the sciences, understood as the terminal discipline because it is the most complex and the most dependent on its predecessors. This paper argues that the canonical reading misidentifies the structural role sociology plays in Comte’s system. A careful rereading, combined with a formal framework developed in recent work on coherence and structural persistence, supports an alternative thesis: sociology is not the apex of the epistemic ladder but its
foundation
—the instance that determines, for any given community, which claims will be treated as real and which will be ignored and erased. Correctness plays only a secondary role in this determination; coherence plays a substantial one, and the coherence-persistence framework adopted here explains both facts. Knowledge without social persistence is not knowledge in any scientifically tractable sense; it is a private cognitive state structurally indistinguishable, at the level of collective inquiry, from the absence of that state. We formalize this intuition by modeling scientific knowledge as a persistent structure across a composite system comprising the individual, the stabilizing artifacts, the community, and the transmission channels, and by proving a Social Indistinguishability Theorem: in the absence of social persistence, the likelihood ratio between “the agent knows
” and “the agent does not know
” converges to unity for any external epistemic observer. A corollary gives the paper its slogan:
a thrice-Einstein without community is indistinguishable from a non-Einstein
. The result is then used to diagnose several open problems in contemporary philosophy of science and philosophy of mind, including the stalemate in scientific realism, the structural prospects of artificial agents as epistemic carriers, and the ongoing dispute concerning the scientific status of the concept of consciousness. {"url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.11003v1.pdf", "scope": "bounded PDF text extraction from up to 24 pages; figures, tables, equations, layout, and scanned-image text may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Stochastic Model for Sunk Cost Bias ∗
Jon Kleinberg1, Sigal Oren 2, Manish Raghavan1, and Nadav Sklar 2
1Computer Science Dept., Cornell University, Ithaca, New York, USA
2Computer Science Dept., Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Be’er Sheva, Israel
June 22, 2021
Abstract
We present a novel model for capturing the behavior of an agent exhibiting sunk-cost
bias in a stochastic environment. Agents exhibiting sunk-cost bias take into account the
eﬀort they have already spent on an endeavor when they evaluate whether to continue
or abandon it. We model planning tasks in which an agent with this type of bias tries
to reach a designated goal. Our model structures this problem as a type of Markov
decision process: loosely speaking, the agent traverses a directed acyclic graph with
probabilistic transitions, paying costs for its actions as it tries to reach a target node
containing a speciﬁed reward. The agent’s sunk cost bias is modeled by a cost that it
incurs for abandoning the traversal: if the agent decides to stop traversing the graph,
it incurs a cost of λ·Csunk, where λ≥ 0 is a parameter that captures the extent of the
bias and Csunk is the sum of costs already invested.
We analyze the behavior of two types of agents: naive agents that are unaware
of their bias, and sophisticated agents that are aware of it. Since optimal (bias-free)
behavior in this problem can involve abandoning the traversal before reaching the
goal, the bias exhibited by these types of agents can result in sub-optimal behavior
by shifting their decisions about abandonment. We show that in contrast to optimal
agents, it is computationally hard to compute the optimal policy for a sophisticated
agent. Our main results quantify the loss exhibited by these two types of agents with
respect to an optimal agent. We present both general and topology-speciﬁc bounds.
